passage: I'm Omkar, Harsha's roommate in the hostel, and I notice things at night. Around eleven Harsha lies down with the phone held above the face, thumbs sliding. I catch glimpses: a classmate on a beach, a cousin's wedding, someone's offer letter. The sighs get longer. Last night Harsha said, "Everyone is moving ahead and I'm standing here." I don't know what was going on inside that head, only that the mood dropped. I said those pictures were the best ten seconds of a person's week. Harsha snorted but did not argue. This morning I found a daily limit set on the phone and the phone on the shelf, and we went to the canteen for breakfast without it.

qa.q: Where do Omkar and Harsha live together?
qa.a: Omkar and Harsha are roommates in the hostel.

qa.q: What might Harsha be feeling as the sighs get longer, and how sure can Omkar be?
qa.a: Behind and discouraged, judging by the sighs and the remark about everyone moving ahead, but Omkar admits not knowing what was going on inside.

qa.q: What small step did Harsha take, and why might it help?
qa.a: Setting a daily limit and putting the phone on the shelf, because less scrolling means fewer highlight reels to compare with.

qa.q: Why might Omkar have called the pictures the best ten seconds of a person's week?
qa.a: To remind Harsha gently that posts show highlights, not whole lives, without lecturing.

grounding: A young adult scrolls through friends' milestones and feels behind, then limits phone time.

passage:
Sunday night. Francis scrolled for an hour through friends' holidays, a wedding in Goa and Riya's new job, and felt like the only person standing still. Sleep came late.
Tuesday. In the canteen Mohit showed the holiday photos and laughed, "You should have seen the bus breakdown and the two-hour argument about money." Francis realised the pictures showed the sunset, not the argument.
Saturday. Francis set a daily limit on the phone, muted two accounts that made the chest go tight, and spent the afternoon at the cricket nets with Mohit. The next Sunday there was still some scrolling, but only ten minutes of it, and breakfast felt lighter.

qa.q: What did Mohit say happened on the holiday besides the sunset?
qa.a: Mohit mentioned the bus breakdown and the two-hour argument about money.

qa.q: What did Francis feel on Sunday night?
qa.a: Left behind; an hour of holidays, a wedding and a job announcement made Francis feel like the only person standing still.

qa.q: Which changes helped Francis's mood?
qa.a: Setting a daily limit and muting two accounts, plus spending time in person with Mohit.

qa.q: How might the holiday photos look from Mohit's side?
qa.a: Mohit remembers the whole trip, including the breakdown and the argument, so the photos are only the pleasant part.

grounding: A young adult feels behind after friends' posts, learns they show highlights only, and limits scrolling.

passage:
"Suraj. It's one in the morning. Why is your face blue?"
"Go to sleep, Sachin."
"You're scrolling again."
Suraj sat up. "Look at this. Anushka, from our batch. Internship in Singapore. Karan got engaged. Pooja's on a beach somewhere. And I'm here, failing thermodynamics, in a room that smells of your socks."
"Hey. The socks are washed."
"You know what I mean. Everyone's ahead."
Sachin propped up on an elbow. "Karan also cried in the corridor about his placement last month. Did he post that?"
"No."
"Pooja posted the beach. Not the fight with her parents to go."
Suraj was quiet. "So it's only the good bits."
"It's always only the good bits. Give me that." Sachin held out his hand. "Phone on my table till breakfast. Deal?"
Suraj hesitated, then passed it over. He lay down and stared at the ceiling fan, heart still racing, but slower.

qa.q: What time was it when Sachin spoke to Suraj?
qa.a: It was one in the morning.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel while scrolling through the posts?
qa.a: Suraj felt behind and inadequate, comparing himself with friends' internships, engagements and holidays while failing a subject.

qa.q: What did Sachin suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Sachin asked for the phone until breakfast, which limits late-night scrolling, and reminded Suraj that posts show only the good bits.

qa.q: How does Sachin see his friends' posts differently from Suraj?
qa.a: Sachin knows the hard parts behind them, like Karan crying about placement, so he sees the posts as highlights rather than whole lives.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who scrolls through friends' news and feels behind, and a friend who reminds him posts are highlights and limits his screen time.

passage:
Looking back, last winter was the worst of it. I had graduated, I was back at my parents' house in Nagpur, sending applications into silence. Every night I would open the photo app and scroll. A school friend's wedding in Udaipur. Someone's first salary treat. Someone's flat with plants. Each one felt like a small slap. By midnight I would be convinced I, Suraj, was the only failure left in the whole batch.
It was my cousin Hemant who said something. We were on the terrace and he'd seen me refreshing. "You know my wedding photos?" he said. "We fought in the car for an hour before those." I laughed, then felt odd.
So I tried something small. The app got a thirty-minute limit, and I stopped opening it after dinner. It didn't fix the job hunt. But my evenings stopped ending in that heavy, sinking feeling. I got a job in March.

qa.q: What limit did Suraj put on the app?
qa.a: A thirty-minute limit, and no opening it after dinner.

qa.q: How did the posts make Suraj feel by midnight?
qa.a: Each post felt like a small slap, and by midnight Suraj felt like the only failure left in the batch.

qa.q: Which choice helped Suraj, and why?
qa.a: Limiting time on the app and stopping after dinner cut down the comparing, so evenings no longer ended in a sinking mood, even though the job hunt went on.

qa.q: How might Hemant have seen Suraj refreshing the phone?
qa.a: Hemant probably felt concerned and understanding, and shared the car fight to show that even happy photos hide hard moments.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who compares himself with friends' posts, feels behind, and helps his mood by limiting time and remembering posts show highlights.

passage:
Mentor's note, second-year counselling hour, Wednesday.
Leela came in for the routine check-in but kept glancing at the phone face-down on the desk. When I asked how the term was going, Leela said, "Fine," and then, after a pause, "Everyone else seems to have their life sorted." Leela showed me the posts: a classmate's paid internship, a cousin's engagement, a friend's trip to the hills. Leela's voice dropped with each one. Leela said the scrolling started after dinner and went on past two.
I asked what Leela's own last week looked like. It included a debate win and helping a friend, Kiran, move hostels. None of it had been posted. We talked about highlight reels, and Leela laughed a little at that. We agreed on one experiment: no scrolling after eleven for a week, and one line a day in a notebook about something real. Follow-up set for next Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Leela's own last week include?
qa.a: It included a debate win and helping a friend, Kiran, move hostels.

qa.q: How was Leela feeling when showing the mentor the posts?
qa.a: Leela felt discouraged and behind, the voice dropping with each post and saying everyone else seemed to have life sorted.

qa.q: What experiment did they agree on, and why might it help?
qa.a: No scrolling after eleven for a week and writing one real thing a day; it limits comparison and reminds Leela of an actual life that isn't posted.

qa.q: How might Kiran see Leela's week compared with Leela's view?
qa.a: Kiran would probably remember Leela as a helpful friend who made a hard move easier, which is far from being behind.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who feels behind after scrolling friends' news and, with a mentor, remembers that posts show highlights and limits screen time.

passage:
Tenzin's journal, Thursday, 1 am.
Scrolled for two hours. Rohit's in Bali. Urmila got the consulting job. Three weddings. Someone from school bought a car. I'm in my hostel room eating instant noodles, still waiting on two internship replies, and I felt like I'd been left on the platform while the train pulled out.
Then I remembered Urmila calling me last month, crying, because she'd been rejected six times before this job. None of that is on her page. Just the offer letter and a cake.
Everyone posts the cake. Nobody posts the six rejections.
New rule for me: phone goes in the drawer at eleven. No scrolling before breakfast. I moved the app off my home screen tonight.
Tomorrow I'll call Urmila and say congratulations properly, on the phone, not with a heart.
Also, I should sleep.

qa.q: What time does Tenzin's phone now go in the drawer?
qa.a: The phone goes in the drawer at eleven.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel while scrolling?
qa.a: Tenzin felt left behind and low, like being left on the platform while the train pulled out.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin see the posts differently?
qa.a: Remembering Urmila's six rejections behind one happy post showed that pages show only the highlights.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Tenzin calls to congratulate her properly?
qa.a: Urmila would probably feel warmly supported, since Tenzin knows the hard road behind the offer and not just the cake 😊

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who scrolls through friends' highlights and feels behind, then remembers that posts hide the hard parts and sets limits on phone time.
